examDifficulty.heading: Is the Tableau Desktop Foundations Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: This is the gentlest Tableau exam. It asks what the tool does and where things live, rather than making you design a data model or write complex calculations. If you have built a few dashboards yourself, most of it will look familiar.
bullets: 40 questions in 70 minutes, which is a comfortable pace.
48% to pass, about 20 correct answers out of 40. Confirm it in the official exam guide before you book, since Salesforce updates these.
Wide but shallow. Connecting to data, chart types, the Marks card, filters, simple calculations and dashboards.
Practice beats reading. Two to four weeks of building in Tableau Desktop is usually enough.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: You are ready when you can connect to a spreadsheet. Build a bar and a line chart, add a filter. Write a simple calculated field and put two sheets on a dashboard without looking anything up. Aim for 80% or more on practice tests.

examFormat.heading: Tableau Desktop Foundations Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: You can take the exam online with a proctor or at a test centre. Here is what to expect:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Many questions describe a small task, such as showing sales by region or highlighting the top five products, and ask which feature does it.
bestWayToPass: Know dimensions from measures: Dimensions describe things and slice the view. Measures are numbers that get added up.
Learn the Marks card: Colour, Size, Label, Detail and Tooltip each change the view differently. Dragging a field to Detail splits the marks without changing colour.
Practise filters and sorting: Filter on a dimension, filter on a measure, and sort by a field rather than by hand.
Build one real dashboard: Put two sheets together, add a filter, and make the filter apply to both.

certificationCard.description: This entry-level exam covers the basics of Tableau Desktop: connecting to data, building charts, filtering and sorting, writing simple calculations, and putting sheets together into a dashboard. The exam is 40 scored questions in 70 minutes, with a 48% pass mark, weighted towards Exploring and Analyzing Data (37%) and Sharing Insights (25%).

keyConcepts.h2: Tableau Desktop Foundations: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Connecting to Data
blocks.body: Tableau Desktop connects to files such as Excel and CSV, to databases, and to published sources on Tableau Server or Tableau Cloud. Once connected, you can join tables, which combines columns from two tables on a matching field, or union them, which stacks rows from tables with the same columns. A **live connection** queries the source each time, so the view always shows current data. An **extract** takes a copy into Tableau's own fast format, which helps with slow sources and lets you work offline. In the data pane, fields arrive as **dimensions** (things to slice by, like Region or Order Date) or **measures** (numbers to aggregate, like Sales). You can change a field's data type and rename it without touching the source.

blocks.heading: Building Views: Rows, Columns and the Marks Card
blocks.body: A view is built by putting fields on **Rows** and **Columns**. Tableau decides the chart type from what you drop, and the **Show Me** panel suggests charts that fit the fields you have selected, greying out the ones that need different fields. The **Marks card** controls how the marks look: **Colour** splits and colours them, **Size** scales them, **Label** writes values on them, **Tooltip** sets what appears on hover, and **Detail** splits marks into more pieces without changing their appearance. Measures are aggregated by default, usually as a sum, and you can change that to average, count or minimum from the field's menu.

blocks.heading: Filtering, Sorting and Grouping
blocks.body: **Dimension filters** keep or exclude categories. **Measure filters** keep rows inside a numeric range. A **Top N filter** keeps, say, the five best products by sales. You can show a filter on screen as a **quick filter** so viewers change it themselves, and decide whether it applies to one sheet or to every sheet using that data source. **Sorting** can be alphabetical, by a measure, or manual. **Groups** combine several members into one, for example rolling small categories into Other, while **sets** are a saved selection you can use in calculations and filters. **Hierarchies** let viewers drill from Country to State to City.

blocks.heading: Calculated Fields
blocks.body: A **calculated field** makes a new field from existing ones. The common kinds are arithmetic (Profit divided by Sales for a margin), string functions such as LEFT or CONTAINS, date functions such as DATEDIFF or DATEPART, and logic with IF or CASE, for example flagging orders above a value as High. **Aggregate** functions like SUM and AVG work on the whole group of rows behind a mark, so you cannot mix an aggregated and a non-aggregated field in the same expression. Tableau also offers quick **table calculations** such as running total, percent of total and difference, which compute on what is already in the view rather than in the source data.

blocks.heading: Dashboards and Stories
blocks.body: A **dashboard** brings several sheets into one screen. Objects can be **tiled**, which snaps them into a layout that resizes neatly, or **floating**, which you position freely. **Dashboard actions** make the dashboard interactive: a **filter action** uses a selection in one sheet to filter another, a **highlight action** emphasises matching marks, and a **URL action** opens a link. A **story** is a sequence of sheets or dashboards with captions, used to walk an audience through a finding step by step. Finished work is shared by publishing it to Tableau Cloud or Tableau Server.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Tableau Desktop Foundations Exam
scenarioTips.intro: Most questions name a small task and ask which feature does it. Learn where each control lives and what it changes in the view.

blocks.heading: Connecting to Data
blocks.body: Joins add columns, unions add rows. Live connections stay current, extracts are faster and work offline.

blocks.heading: Building Views
blocks.body: Show Me suggests charts for the fields you picked. Measures aggregate by default, usually as a sum.

blocks.heading: Sorting and Grouping
blocks.body: Sort by a measure rather than by hand. Groups combine members, sets save a selection, hierarchies allow drilling.

blocks.heading: Calculations
blocks.body: Simple arithmetic, string, date and IF logic cover most of the exam. Table calculations work on what is in the view.

blocks.heading: Dashboards and Sharing
blocks.body: Use a filter action to make one sheet filter another, and publish to Tableau Cloud or Server to share.

sampleQuestions.question: You need to combine a sales table and a returns table that share an Order ID column, so the returns information appears alongside each order. What should you use?
options: A union of the two tables
sampleQuestions.explanation: A join matches rows using a shared field and brings the other table's columns alongside, which is what is needed here.
whyWrong: A filter action links sheets in a dashboard, not tables in a data source.
A calculated field works with data you already have.
A union stacks rows from tables with the same columns. It does not add columns.

sampleQuestions.question: Monthly sales files all have identical columns, and you want them all in one data source as additional rows. What should you use?
sampleQuestions.explanation: A union stacks rows from tables with the same structure, which is what you want for repeated monthly files.
whyWrong: Groups combine members of a field, not tables.
Sets save a selection of members.
A join would add columns rather than stack rows.

sampleQuestions.question: Which statement about dimensions and measures is correct?
options: Dimensions are always dates; measures are always text
Measures slice the view; dimensions are aggregated
They are interchangeable and behave identically
sampleQuestions.explanation: Dimensions are the descriptive fields you break the view down by. Measures are numeric fields that Tableau aggregates, usually by summing them.
whyWrong: Dimensions can be text, dates or numbers, and measures are numeric, not text.
That reverses the two roles.
They behave differently, which is why Tableau separates them.

sampleQuestions.question: A scatter plot shows one mark per region, but you want one mark per customer while keeping the colour as it is. Where should you drag the Customer field?
options: The Colour shelf on the Marks card
sampleQuestions.explanation: Detail splits the marks into more pieces without changing how they look, which is exactly the requirement.
whyWrong: Filters would remove data rather than split marks.
Colour would split the marks and recolour them, changing the appearance.
Columns would change the chart's structure.

sampleQuestions.question: You want the view to show only the five products with the highest sales. What is the simplest way?
options: A Top N filter on Product by sum of Sales
Sorting the products and leaving the rest visible
A measure filter on Sales above a guessed value
sampleQuestions.explanation: A Top N filter keeps the highest five by the measure you choose, and it updates as the data changes.
whyWrong: Hiding by hand breaks as soon as the data changes.
Sorting changes the order but still shows every product.
A guessed threshold may return more or fewer than five.

sampleQuestions.question: A viewer should be able to change the Region shown on a published dashboard. What should you add?
options: A separate calculated field for each region
A quick filter shown on the dashboard
sampleQuestions.explanation: Showing the filter puts a control on screen so viewers pick the region themselves.
whyWrong: Calculated fields do not give the viewer a control.
A group combines members rather than offering a choice.
One dashboard per region is unnecessary duplication.

sampleQuestions.question: One filter should apply to every sheet built on the same data source, not just the current sheet. What should you do?
options: Apply it to all sheets using that source
Copy the filter onto each sheet by hand
Put the filter on the Detail shelf
Convert the filter into a set
sampleQuestions.explanation: A filter's scope can be widened so it applies to all worksheets using that data source, keeping sheets in step.
whyWrong: Copying by hand works but has to be repeated and drifts out of step.
Detail splits marks and has nothing to do with filter scope.
A set saves a selection but does not apply a filter everywhere.

sampleQuestions.question: You need a field that shows profit as a percentage of sales. What should you create?
options: A Top N filter on Profit
A union joined to the profit table
A field dividing SUM(Profit) by SUM(Sales)
sampleQuestions.explanation: A calculated field with aggregated measures gives the ratio correctly for whatever level the view shows.
whyWrong: A Top N filter selects members rather than calculating.
A union stacks rows and does not compute a ratio.
Groups combine members of a dimension.

sampleQuestions.question: Several small product categories should be reported together as Other. What feature fits?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Groups combine several members of a field into one, which is how you roll small categories into Other.
whyWrong: A set is a saved selection used in filters and calculations.
A hierarchy lets viewers drill between levels.
An extract is a copy of the data for speed.

sampleQuestions.question: A database is slow and you also want to work on the dashboard while travelling without a connection. What should you use?
sampleQuestions.explanation: An extract copies the data into Tableau's own format, which is faster and works offline.
whyWrong: A live connection queries the source every time and needs the connection.
A story sequences sheets for presenting.
A union combines rows and does not change performance this way.

sampleQuestions.question: What does a filter action on a dashboard do?
options: Permanently removes the rows from the data source
Uses a selection in one sheet to filter another sheet
Publishes the dashboard to Tableau Cloud
Creates a calculated field from the selection
sampleQuestions.explanation: Filter actions make dashboards interactive: clicking a mark in one sheet filters the others.
whyWrong: Nothing is removed from the underlying data.
Publishing is a separate step.
No calculated field is created.

sampleQuestions.question: You want to walk an audience through a finding one step at a time, with a caption on each step. What should you build?
sampleQuestions.explanation: A story is a sequence of sheets or dashboards with captions, designed for presenting a narrative.
whyWrong: Sets save selections.
Hierarchies are for drilling into levels of detail.
A dashboard shows views together rather than in sequence.

sampleQuestions.question: Viewers should be able to drill from Country down to State and then City in one click. What should you create?
sampleQuestions.explanation: A hierarchy nests the fields so viewers can expand from one level to the next in the view.
whyWrong: Separate sheets make the viewer navigate manually.
A group combines members rather than nesting levels.
A measure filter limits numeric ranges.

sampleQuestions.question: Sales is showing as a sum, but you need the average order value in the view instead. What should you change?
options: The mark type to a line
The data type of the field
sampleQuestions.explanation: A measure's aggregation can be changed from the field's menu, which switches the view from total to average.
whyWrong: Mark type changes the chart's appearance.
The data type controls how the field is interpreted, not how it is aggregated.
Layout affects positioning on a dashboard.

sampleQuestions.question: What does the Show Me panel do?
options: Creates an extract of the data source
Publishes the workbook for others to view
Writes a calculated field for you
Suggests charts suited to the selected fields
sampleQuestions.explanation: Show Me offers chart types that work with the fields you picked, and greys out those that need different fields.
whyWrong: Extracts are created from the data source menu.
Publishing is done separately to Tableau Cloud or Server.
Calculations are written by you in the calculation editor.
